title: Speed to power: solutions to US data centres’ challenges | Wood Mackenzie
gist: US data centre demand is racing ahead of power supply, with 201 GW of committed load facing grid waits of 54-84 months and 278-week gas turbine queues. Simon Flowers sees no meaningful new supply in 2027-28 and points to behind-the-meter gas, ERCOT-style planning and flexible demand as partial fixes.

themes.theme: Scale of US data centre buildout

insights.claim: Hyperscaler capital expenditure has increased four-fold since 2023 and is set to exceed US$750 billion this year, more than global spend on renewable power or upstream oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Capex scale shows AI power demand is a capital-allocation force larger than whole energy sub-sectors.
insights.locator: How best to measure the breakneck pace

insights.claim: Hyperscaler electricity consumption has grown 23% a year this decade, while total US power demand did not grow from 2006 to 2024.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Marks a structural break from two decades of flat load; supports utility and generation growth theses.
insights.locator: Hyperscaler electricity consumption is another metric

insights.claim: US utilities have committed to connect 201 GW of new data centre capacity, which would raise electricity demand by 30% if all of it is built.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: The 201 GW queue is the key volume to track for power-sector earnings and capacity needs.
insights.locator: 201 GW of new data centre capacity

insights.claim: Grid connection waits for data centres keep lengthening: at best 54 months in Virginia and 84 months in Ohio, meaning no power until 2033 for an Ohio project starting today.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Interconnection delay, not demand, is the binding constraint; favours sites and developers with power already secured.
insights.locator: First, the timetable for getting a data centre connected

insights.claim: Lawmakers have called 400 moratoriums on data centre proposals, and one-fifth of projects under development have been delayed by at least one.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Rising public opposition adds political risk to data centre pipelines and timelines.
insights.locator: Second, public opposition to data centre development

insights.claim: Heavy frame gas turbine waitlists have stretched to 278 weeks (roughly early 2032), with transformers at 162 weeks and circuit breakers at 137 weeks, so developers not early in the queue cannot deliver gas power before 2030.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Equipment makers with scarce capacity hold pricing power; late orderers face multi-year delays.
insights.locator: Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply

insights.claim: Skilled labour is emerging as a further bottleneck in power build-out that cannot be solved quickly.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Labour scarcity adds cost and schedule risk to grid and generation projects.
insights.locator: Skilled labourers are also emerging as a bottleneck

insights.claim: Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Supports demand for gas turbines and gas supply tied to data centre load.
insights.locator: Gas-fired power plants will dominate data centre power supply

insights.claim: No solution delivers new power supply at meaningful scale in 2027 or 2028 beyond what is already committed; the goal is to have supply connected by the time demand ramps beyond 2028.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Expect a power shortfall window through 2028, supporting scarcity pricing for existing and committed capacity.
insights.locator: Realistically, there are no solutions that deliver new supply

insights.claim: Industry should focus on delivering the 201 GW already committed, because adding more capacity to the pipeline before the logjam clears will only hinder progress.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Argues against queue expansion; pipeline numbers may overstate near-term deliverable load.
insights.locator: And the focus should be on delivering the 201 GW

insights.claim: Behind-the-meter projects are 15% of the data centre pipeline by project count but 40% of planned capacity, and skip grid connection and its regulatory hurdles.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Large projects are disproportionately going off-grid, a growth niche for onsite gas and batteries.

insights.claim: Most behind-the-meter plans will be gas-fired capacity backed increasingly by new high-discharge batteries; they are expensive and complex, and few data centres see them as a long-term plan versus eventual grid connection.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: BTM is a bridge solution; demand for onsite gas and batteries may be transitional.
insights.locator: Most BTM plans will be gas-fired capacity

insights.claim: The ERCOT approach of analysing planned large-load locations, assuming where generation will be built and making an 80/20 transmission investment decision is a pragmatic model for unregulated markets.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Texas-style planning may speed interconnection; watch other markets copying it.
insights.locator: The ‘ERCOT solution’ could be a pragmatic way forward

insights.claim: Demand interruptibility is emerging as a solution, with developers exploring how BTM generators or batteries could give the grid flexibility and deregulated market rules evolving to allow flexible interconnect.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Flexible-load rules could accelerate connections and create value for storage and onsite assets.
insights.locator: Interruptibility of demand is emerging as another solution

insights.claim: Unregulated markets let data centres choose suppliers and build BTM generation, but suffer a disconnect between large-load planning and generation interconnection planning, with many independent decisions hindering cost-effective grid build-out.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Fragmented planning raises risk of supply lagging demand in merchant regions.
insights.locator: Unregulated markets are easier in some ways

insights.claim: Regulated markets can mitigate some planning uncertainty and grid inefficiency.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Regulated-utility regions may offer more predictable data centre delivery.
insights.locator: Regulated markets can mitigate some of the planning uncertainty

insights.claim: Hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive, which regulated utilities can leverage to address affordability concerns and fund faster connection or new technologies such as advanced geothermal and long-duration energy storage.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler willingness to pay could pull forward emerging generation and storage technologies.
insights.locator: Yes. For one thing, hyperscalers are currently price-insensitive

insights.claim: After decades in a low-growth bubble, utilities are devising solutions for large-load customers on already constrained grids.
insights.speaker: Simon Flowers
insights.so_what: Signals a shift from low-growth to growth-oriented utility strategy.
insights.locator: After operating in a low-growth bubble for decades
